title: I celebrate myself
hook: a poet opens his book by praising himself, then hands every atom of it to you
tomorrow: a child hands him grass and asks what it is. what does he say?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Blake's little verse: bind a joy to yourself and you lose it; kiss it as it flies. Joy held loosely. Today, a poet who held nothing back about himself.
screen: `KISS IT AS IT FLIES.` → `NOTHING HELD BACK.`

segments.voice: A friend posts a birthday carousel, all selfies, captioned main character era, and the group chat goes quiet in that particular way. Too much? Now a print shop in Brooklyn. A tall man in a work shirt, hat tipped back, is getting his own book of poems ready. No author's name on the title page. Just an engraving of him, collar open, one hand on his hip, like a laborer between jobs. And the long poem inside begins: "I celebrate myself."
screen: `MAIN CHARACTER ERA?` → `A PRINT SHOP IN BROOKLYN.` → `NO NAME ON THE TITLE PAGE.` → `I CELEBRATE MYSELF.`

segments.voice: It sounds like that carousel, long before phones. In later editions he made the line even bolder: "I celebrate myself, and sing myself." Then, in the very next breath, Whitman turns it inside out: "And what I assume you shall assume, For every atom belonging to me as good belongs to you." He isn't celebrating himself instead of you. He's celebrating himself as you: the same atoms, the same breath, the same grass underfoot. Later he names himself: "Walt Whitman, a kosmos, of Manhattan the son." A kosmos is a whole ordered world. And his I keeps widening. "I am of old and young, of the foolish as much as the wise," he says, and he goes on: parent and child, Northerner and Southerner, a boatman on the lakes. That's the teaching of the poem's opening. The self, looked at honestly and loved, isn't a wall around one person. It's a door into everyone. Some readers call it a democratic faith: nobody outside the circle, nobody above it. So the difference from vanity is the direction. Vanity says: look at me, not you. Whitman says: look at me, and you'll find yourself.
screen: `EVERY ATOM BELONGS TO YOU AS WELL.` · `WALT WHITMAN, A KOSMOS.` · `OLD AND YOUNG, FOOLISH AND WISE.` · `THE SELF IS A DOOR, NOT A WALL.` · then, large: `I CELEBRATE MYSELF.`

segments.voice: Choose one ordinary thing about you: your hands, your laugh, the way you make coffee. Say it out loud, plainly, the way Whitman would: I celebrate my hands. Then let it widen, quietly: hands like these are working all over the world right now.
I celebrate myself: the opening of Whitman's Song of Myself, where praising one ordinary self opens out into everyone, every atom shared.
Your line: I celebrate myself. And what I assume, you shall assume. See you tomorrow.

fork.setup: a friend says Whitman's opening is just ego, the first selfie. what's Whitman's best answer, from the poem itself?

chat.meaning: Whitman's 'I celebrate myself' turns at once: what I assume you shall assume. Celebrating a self is celebrating what everyone shares.
